package_info.package_name: N/A (RepoJacking vulnerability affects any package using a renamed GitHub username)
package_info.package_manager: Go, Swift, Packagist (and any manager using GitHub URLs as source)
package_info.package_versions: All versions referencing vulnerable (renamed) GitHub repositories
package_info.why_malicious: The vulnerability enables attackers to hijack the namespace of popular repositories after a username change on GitHub. By recreating a repository under a reclaimed username, attackers can serve malicious code to users and automated systems that depend on the original repository URL. This constitutes a supply chain attack vector capable of poisoning packages and GitHub Actions at scale, leading to widespread compromise.

execution_context.trigger: Repository namespace hijack following a GitHub username rename
execution_context.file_location: Attacker-controlled repository at the hijacked namespace (e.g., github.com/old-username/repo)
required_permissions: Ability to register a previously used GitHub username
Ability to create a repository with the same name as the original
Ability to push code to the new repository

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Attacker creates a repository with the same name as the original under a reclaimed username, then pushes malicious code. For example, if the original repository was at github.com/old-username/repo and the owner renames their username, the attacker registers 'old-username', creates 'repo', and pushes code that may contain backdoors, credential stealers, or other malicious payloads.
malicious_snippets.code_language: Any (depends on the original repository's language, e.g., Go, PHP, Swift, YAML for GitHub Actions)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: When a user or package manager fetches or installs from the hijacked repository URL, the system retrieves attacker-controlled code, which may execute arbitrary logic, exfiltrate data, or introduce supply chain compromise.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Recreation of a previously retired repository namespace by a new owner, especially with a different commit history or codebase, is a strong indicator of a supply chain attack. The attacker can introduce malicious code that is automatically trusted by users and systems relying on the original repository URL.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Users and automated systems expect the repository URL to always resolve to the original, trusted codebase. RepoJacking breaks this trust by allowing a new, untrusted party to control the namespace and serve arbitrary code, violating the integrity and authenticity of the supply chain.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate repository transfers or username changes may occur, but these are typically accompanied by clear communication and do not involve serving unrelated or malicious code. Legitimate use never involves silently replacing trusted code with attacker-controlled payloads.
key_indicators: A repository at a previously retired namespace reappears with a new owner and a different commit history
Sudden introduction of unexpected, obfuscated, or unrelated code in a repository at a popular namespace
Repository owner history shows recent username rename and transfer activity, followed by recreation of the original namespace
Automated systems or package managers begin fetching code from a repository with a recent ownership change

attack_chain.action: Attacker registers a GitHub username that was previously used by a popular repository owner who renamed their account.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker can now create a repository with the same name as the original under the reclaimed username.

attack_chain.action: Attacker creates a repository with the same name as the original (e.g., 'repo') under the hijacked username.
attack_chain.leads_to: Repository URL now points to attacker-controlled code.

attack_chain.action: Attacker pushes malicious code to the new repository, which may include backdoors, credential stealers, or other supply chain threats.
attack_chain.leads_to: Any user or package manager fetching from the original URL receives attacker-supplied malicious code.

attack_chain.action: Malicious code is distributed to users via package managers, CI/CD pipelines, or direct git clone/install commands.
attack_chain.leads_to: Potential compromise of user systems, supply chain poisoning, or further downstream attacks.

behavioral_signatures: A repository at a previously retired namespace reappears with a new owner
Significant changes in repository commit history or codebase at a popular namespace
Repository owner history shows recent username rename and transfer activity, followed by recreation of the original namespace
Automated systems or package managers begin fetching code from a repository with a recent ownership change
file_indicators: Repository files at a namespace that was previously retired and is now owned by a different user
Unexpected or obfuscated code in newly created repositories at popular or previously trusted namespaces
Absence of expected commit history or release tags in a repository that was previously popular
network_indicators: Package manager or CI/CD systems fetching code from a namespace with recent ownership changes
Unusual spikes in downloads or clones from a newly created repository at a popular namespace
Automated build or deployment systems accessing repositories with a recent change in owner or commit history
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Continuously monitor for the recreation of repositories at previously retired namespaces, especially following a username rename. Alert on any repository that appears at a namespace with a history of high popularity but a new owner or commit history. Compare commit histories and codebases for significant, unexplained changes. Package managers and CI/CD systems should validate repository owner history, enforce the use of immutable commit hashes or tags, and avoid relying solely on username/repo combinations. Implement automated alerts for ownership changes and repository recreations at high-value namespaces.
